newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel sticks to deficit goal despite tax changes.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sticks to deficit goal despite tax changes.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Friday that his budget deficit target for 1997 remained intact after tax changes agreed by the country's centre-right coalition government.

"We will have no higher deficit," Waigel told reporters. He has set a goal of cutting the deficit next year to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, within the three percent limit set by the Maastricht treaty to qualify for the planned launch of a single currency in 1999.
Waigel said current estimates showed a combined deficit of 105 billion marks in 1997 for federal and state governments.

He said the coalition's decision to delay a cut in the solidarity surcharge would bring about 3.7 billion marks to government coffers, nearly offsetting the four billion marks lost by the accelerated increase in government child benefits.
A further three billion marks in spending cuts will need to be found in 1997, but the government will seek to spare investment outlays from the austerity pressures.

Still, Waigel said he sees little room to cut spending in the defence, transport or research ministries, or in social spending such as unemployment. He said the government would discuss whether to stick by the planned January 1999 start of its comprehensive tax reform plan.
